_about: Demo J (quantum crypto dependency explorer). Single source for the static HTML in m10.html (written by scripts/invisible_engine/content/inserts.py) and for explorer.js; tested by invisible-engine/tests/demos.mjs. Status: shor = would fail on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer (none is publicly known to exist); grover = weakened only in an idealised count; pq = designed to resist known quantum attacks; mixed = parts of each.

statuses.shor: Would fail on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer. None is publicly known to exist.
statuses.grover: Weakened only in an idealised count. Not broken.
statuses.pq: Designed to resist known quantum attacks. Runs on ordinary chips.
statuses.mixed: Several parts with different exposure: look at each one.

items.label: RSA
items.kind: Public-key encryption and signatures, resting on the difficulty of factoring.
items.where: Card certificates for offline data authentication; older TLS certificates (Scenes 14, 73).
items.impact: Shor’s algorithm factors efficiently on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer.
items.caveats: Published resource estimates for RSA-2048 keep falling (about 20 million noisy qubits in 2019; under a million in 2025) but remain estimates, and dated ones.
items.next: ML-KEM for key establishment, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA for signatures; first find where RSA actually lives.

items.label: ECDH / ECDSA
items.kind: Elliptic-curve key agreement and signatures, resting on discrete logarithms.
items.where: Bluetooth LE Secure Connections pairing (P-256), Find My reports (P-224), TLS key exchange (X25519), passkeys (Scenes 44, 73).
items.impact: Shor’s algorithm also solves elliptic-curve discrete logarithms, again only on a large fault-tolerant machine.
items.caveats: Elliptic-curve keys are tiny; their replacements are not (Scene 75), which matters for tags and advertisements.
items.next: Hybrid key establishment (for example X25519 with ML-KEM-768) where the protocol has room; redesign where it does not.

items.label: AES
items.kind: Symmetric block cipher: one shared secret key.
items.where: Card cryptograms on newer cards, Find My report encryption (AES-GCM), disk and backup encryption.
items.impact: Grover’s algorithm gives at most a square-root speed-up in an idealised count: AES-128 to about 2⁶⁴ steps, AES-256 to about 2¹²⁸.
items.caveats: Grover parallelises poorly: splitting the search across k machines saves only √k. Not broken.
items.next: Prefer 256-bit keys for data that must stay secret for decades; no new algorithm needed.

items.label: SHA-2 hashes
items.kind: Hash functions: fingerprints of data, used in signatures, lookups and key derivation.
items.where: Find My lookup values (SHA-256 of the public key), key derivation, firmware digests.
items.impact: Finding a preimage drops to about 2¹²⁸ steps for SHA-256 in an idealised count; collision search gains little in practice.
items.caveats: Not broken. Hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA) are built on exactly this robustness.
items.next: SHA-256 and SHA-384 remain the building blocks of the new standards.

items.label: ML-KEM (FIPS 203)
items.kind: Key-encapsulation mechanism from lattice problems; standardised August 2024.
items.where: Hybrid TLS key exchange already deployed by some browsers and networks (verify current status); future device pairing.
items.impact: No known quantum algorithm breaks it efficiently.
items.caveats: Young implementations: side channels and bugs are the near-term risk. ML-KEM-768 sends a 1,184-byte key and a 1,088-byte ciphertext.
items.next: Use in hybrid with a classical exchange during migration; measure sizes against each link’s limits.

items.label: ML-DSA (FIPS 204)
items.where: Future certificates, firmware signing and accounts.
items.impact: No known quantum algorithm breaks it efficiently.
items.caveats: ML-DSA-65 has a 1,952-byte public key and 3,309-byte signatures: tens of times larger than ECDSA.
items.next: Plan storage, bandwidth and boot-time verification for the larger sizes.

items.label: SLH-DSA (FIPS 205)
items.where: Long-lived roots of trust, such as firmware signing keys.
items.impact: Security rests on hash functions alone, the most conservative choice.
items.caveats: Large, slow signatures: the small variant SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s signs with 7,856 bytes.
items.next: Suited to rare, high-value signatures, not chatty protocols.

items.label: Card payment cryptography
items.kind: Symmetric transaction cryptograms plus public-key certificates for offline checks.
items.impact: The symmetric cryptogram faces only Grover’s idealised speed-up; RSA certificates face Shor at scale.
items.caveats: Card generations and schemes differ; check the scheme’s current specification.
items.next: Cards are reissued every few years, which gives a natural migration path that tags lack.

items.label: Bluetooth LE authentication
items.kind: LE Secure Connections pairing uses elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman on P-256.
items.where: Phone and accessory pairing; owner setup (Module 5).
items.impact: A recorded pairing could be attacked later only with a large fault-tolerant quantum computer, and only if the link protected secrets that still matter.
items.caveats: Advertisements carry no link encryption at all; their privacy comes from rotating identifiers (Scene 28).
items.next: Any post-quantum pairing must fit Bluetooth’s small packets: a protocol change, not a setting.

items.label: Firmware signatures
items.kind: The device checks a signature before installing new software.
items.where: Every tag, phone and reader that accepts updates. The AirTag’s algorithm is not publicly documented.
items.impact: If the scheme is RSA or elliptic-curve, a large fault-tolerant quantum computer could forge updates for devices that still accept them.
items.caveats: A key burned into silicon cannot be changed; devices may outlive their algorithms.
items.next: Updatable roots of trust, and hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA) for long-lived keys.

items.label: Cloud access
items.kind: TLS to the service, plus sign-in with passwords, passkeys or security keys.
items.where: Uploading sealed reports and fetching them (Scenes 36–37); accounts (Module 6).
items.impact: TLS key exchange is elliptic-curve today and is moving to hybrid post-quantum; passkey signatures are elliptic-curve.
items.caveats: Phishing, stolen sessions and shared passwords are not quantum problems and are not fixed by post-quantum cryptography (Scene 88).
items.next: Hybrid TLS where offered; plan passkey and certificate migration with vendors.
